chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Hilal, from Uqbah ibn Khalid, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who said, 'This ship belongs to so-and-so,' but did not specify what is in it, and it contains food. Should the man be given the ship and what is in it? He said: 'It is for the one to whom he bequeathed it, unless the owner is suspected (of having other heirs), and the heirs get nothing.'
From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Abu Jamilah, from al-Mufaddal ibn Salih, who said:

I wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) asking him about a man who bequeathed a sword to a man. The heirs said, 'You only have the iron, not the ornamentation; you have nothing but the iron.' He wrote to me: 'The sword is for him, and its ornamentation.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a bequest of a ship or sword when the contents or accessories are not specified?
ai.summary: These narrations from the chapter on ambiguous bequests (al-wasiyyah al-mubhamah) clarify the principle of 'comprehensive inclusion' (istidlal al-kull bi-l-juz'), where unspecified components or contents are deemed part of the bequeathed item unless explicitly excluded. The first narration highlights the juristic presumption that the testator's intent covers the whole entity, while the second reinforces that functional and decorative elements of an object are inseparable in legal interpretation. This reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on preserving the testator's apparent intent while preventing heirs from arbitrarily fragmenting the bequest.
